issues.title: Large scale blocking of TLS-based censorship circumvention tools in China
issues.body:
Starting from October 3, 2022 (Beijing Time), more than 100 users reported that at least one of their TLS-based censorship circumvention servers had been blocked. The TLS-based circumvention protocols that are reportedly blocked include [trojan](https://github.com/trojan-gfw/trojan), [Xray](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core), [V2Ray TLS+Websocket](https://www.v2fly.org/config/transport/websocket.html), [VLESS](https://www.v2fly.org/config/protocols/vless.html), and [gRPC](https://www.v2fly.org/config/transport/grpc.html). We have not received any report of the blocking of [naiveproxy](https://github.com/klzgrad/naiveproxy) though.

Below are a summary of this blocking event and our conjuncture.

The blocking is done by blocking the specific port that the circumvention services listen on. When the user [change the blocked port](https://gfw.report/blog/ss_tutorial/en/#mitigate-port-blocking-by-having-backup-ports) to a non-blocked port and keep using the circumvention tools, the entire IP addresses may get blocked. It is worth noting that their domain names are not added to GFW's DNS or SNI blacklists.

While most of the users report their port 443 got blocked, a few users reported that their *non-443* port on which circumvention services listen got blocked as well. While most of the blocked servers are in some popular VPSes providers' datacenters (for example, the [bandwagonhost](https://bandwagonhost.com/)), at least one user reported the blocking of a server in residential network in Europe.

In a few cases (not all cases), the blocking seems to be dynamic because the web browser could still access their circumvention ports but not the circumvention tools did not work.

All these observations above strongly indicate that the GFW can indeed accurately identify and block the circumvention services, rather than simply block the port 443, or block the popular VPS providers.

Based on the information collected above, we suspect, without empirical measurement yet, that the blocking is possibly related to the [TLS fingerprints](https://tlsfingerprint.io/) of those circumvention tools. Perhaps developers want to look into [uTLS](https://github.com/refraction-networking/utls). One may also find this [paper reading group](https://github.com/net4people/bbs/issues/54), [this summary](https://gfw.report/blog/v2ray_weaknesses/en/#unique-tls-clienthello-fingerprints), and [this post](https://zhufan.net/2022/06/18/tls%E6%8F%A1%E6%89%8B%E6%8C%87%E7%BA%B9%E6%A3%80%E6%B5%8B%E6%81%B6%E6%84%8F%E8%BD%AF%E4%BB%B6%E6%B5%81%E9%87%8F/) on TLS fingerprint helpful.

We will investigate if the GFW indeed uses the TLS fingerprints sent by these clients to identify circumvention protocols. At the same time, if you have any server being blocked, or if you have any evidence that can corroborate or falsify our hypothesis, we courage you to share your comments publicly or privately. Our private contact information can be found at the footer of [GFW Report](https://gfw.report).

issues.body:
### Integrity requirements

- [x] I have read all the comments in the issue template and ensured that this issue meet the requirements.
- [x] I confirm that I have read the documentation, understand the meaning of all the configuration items I wrote, and did not pile up seemingly useful options or default values.
- [x] I provided the complete config and logs, rather than just providing the truncated parts based on my own judgment.
- [x] I searched issues and did not find any similar issues.
- [x] The problem can be successfully reproduced in the latest Release (v26.11.9)

### Description

Windows 11 24H2 (build 26100.0), IPv6 partially disabled system-wide with `HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\Tcpip6\Parameters\DisabledComponents = 0x28`. The TUN inbound cannot start in v26.11.9 (676eaf6):

```
Failed to start: app/proxyman/inbound: failed to start proxy > proxy/tun: unable to set DNS > Access is denied.
```

The TUN settings contain no IPv6 at all: `gateway` and `autoSystemRoutingTable` are IPv4-only, `dns` is IPv4-only. The same machine and the same config start fine with a locally patched v26.10.31 that skips the IPv6 `SetDNS` call when the config does not ask for IPv6, so the fatal step is exactly the IPv6 DNS setup.

Why v26.11.9 fails, from the code:

- `Start()` calls `t.luid.SetDNS(family, dns, nil)` for both `AF_INET` and `AF_INET6` (proxy/tun/tun_windows.go:234), regardless of what the config asks for.
- An IPv6 failure is only tolerated when `ignored()` returns true (proxy/tun/tun_windows.go:158-165), which requires `ipv6Off()`.
- `ipv6Off()` only accepts bit `0x10` (proxy/tun/tun_windows.go:105-113):

  ```go
  value, _, err := key.GetIntegerValue("DisabledComponents")
  return err == nil && value&0x10 != 0
  ```

- `0x28 = 0x20 | 0x08` therefore counts as "IPv6 is not off": `ignored()` returns false, and the `Access is denied` from `SetDNS(AF_INET6)` aborts `Start()`.

This tolerance used to be config-based: #7325 / #7332 skipped the IPv6 DNS failure when `!address6 && !route6 && !dns6`, with `dns6 := slices.ContainsFunc(dns, netip.Addr.Is6)`. #7341 (commit 2d287bbd) replaced it with the registry-only check and also removed `dns6`. That covers `0x10` / `0xFF`, but not the very common partial values such as `0x28`, where Windows 11 24H2 still refuses to apply IPv6 DNS servers to the Wintun adapter while nothing IPv6 was requested. This is not a regression against a release: the #7332 behaviour never shipped, because #7341 replaced it two days before v26.11.9.

Question: should a config that requests no IPv6 start with `DisabledComponents = 0x28`? Possible directions:

1. Restore the #7332 escape hatch for `SetDNS` in addition to `ignored()`:
   `if family == windows.AF_INET6 && !address6 && !route6 && !dns6 { continue }`
2. Treat an IPv6 `SetDNS` failure as non-fatal when `!dns6` (there is nothing to apply; clearing is best-effort).
3. Broaden `ipv6Off()` to also cover values like `0x28`.

### Reproduction Method

1. On Windows 11 24H2 x64, set `DisabledComponents = 0x28` under `HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\Tcpip6\Parameters` and reboot.
2. Run the config below as administrator: `xray.exe run -c config.json`.
3. The TUN inbound fails to start with `unable to set DNS > Access is denied`.

No server is needed: the failure happens in the TUN inbound's `Start()`, before any outbound is used, so the config only contains a TUN inbound and a `freedom` outbound.

For reference, the environment:

- OS: Microsoft Windows NT 10.0.26100.0 (Windows 11 24H2), x64
- Xray: v26.11.9 (676eaf6); v26.10.31 (a4a3dff) with the same config also fails
- Driver: wintun 0.14 (bundled `wintun.dll`)

issues.title: Tunnel inbound: Close idle fake UDP sockets in TPROXY mode
issues.body:
Fixes #5263 (closed as not planned).

### Problem

With `tproxy` on a Tunnel (dokodemo-door) inbound, replies go through `PacketWriter`. It opens a fake UDP socket bound to each remote address that sends a reply ([dokodemo.go:231-245](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/blob/c456141815359e1d2c00dfc673f5f26adf22fae2/proxy/dokodemo/dokodemo.go#L231-L245)). The sockets are closed only in `Close()` ([:266-273](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/blob/c456141815359e1d2c00dfc673f5f26adf22fae2/proxy/dokodemo/dokodemo.go#L266-L273)), when the UDP session ends ([:189](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/blob/c456141815359e1d2c00dfc673f5f26adf22fae2/proxy/dokodemo/dokodemo.go#L189)).

A cone session ends after its client port has been silent for 2 minutes ([worker.go:397](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/blob/c456141815359e1d2c00dfc673f5f26adf22fae2/app/proxyman/inbound/worker.go#L397)). Only client packets count as activity ([worker.go:200](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/blob/c456141815359e1d2c00dfc673f5f26adf22fae2/app/proxyman/inbound/worker.go#L200)). A P2P application sends from one port to many peers and is never silent for 2 minutes. Its session keeps one fake socket for every peer that ever replied.

On a router with transparent proxy (TPROXY → dokodemo-door) xray grew by about 1450 sockets and 7 MB of RSS per hour: 6524 open fds 4.5 hours after a restart that followed an OOM kill. #5263 shows the same growth.

### Reproduction

`05-xray-fakeudp-repro.sh` (below) runs as a normal user in network namespaces: `unshare -Urn sh 05-xray-fakeudp-repro.sh ./xray 10 300`. The client sends from one UDP port to 10 new peers per second. Every 10th datagram goes to a peer first contacted more than 180 s ago. Peers echo from the address they were sent to. Inbound:

```json
{"listen": "0.0.0.0", "port": 1100, "protocol": "tunnel",
 "settings": {"allowedNetwork": "udp", "followRedirect": true},
 "streamSettings": {"sockopt": {"tproxy": "tproxy"}}}
```

```sh
iptables -t mangle -A PREROUTING -i <client-if> -p udp -j TPROXY --on-port 1100 --tproxy-mark 1
ip rule add fwmark 1 lookup 100
ip route add local 0.0.0.0/0 dev lo table 100
```

### Results

`main` at c456141, linux/amd64, 10 new peers/s, open fds of the xray process:

| time, s | main | with this PR |
|---|---|---|
| 60 | 609 | 609 |
| 120 | 1209 | 1209 |
| 180 | 1809 | 1508 |
| 240 | 2349 | 1501 |
| 300 | 2888 | 1495 |

Both builds: 3000/3000 replies, 120/120 replies from old peers, none from a wrong address.

Router, arm64, v26.7.28 with the same change: 6524 fds and growing before; about 880 without a trend 15 hours later, 575 five days later.

### Change

- `PacketWriter` records when each remote last sent a reply.
- `WriteMultiBuffer`, at most every 30 s, closes and forgets the fake sockets of remotes silent for 2 minutes. The next reply from such a remote opens a new socket through the existing path.
- The socket of the original destination (`w.conn`) is never closed early. Datagrams without a `UDP` address are written to it too ([:255](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/blob/c456141815359e1d2c00dfc673f5f26adf22fae2/proxy/dokodemo/dokodemo.go#L255)). Before, one write error on it closed it for the rest of the session.
- On a write error the map entry is deleted instead of set to `nil`.

The sweep runs on the writer goroutine: no new goroutine, no lock. 2 minutes matches the session timeout in `worker.go`. If replies stop completely, the sweep waits for the next write, which is the old behavior.

### Tests

- `TestSweepIdleClosesOnlyIdleFakeSockets` in `proxy/dokodemo/fakeudp_sweep_test.go`.
- `go build ./...`, `go test ./proxy/dokodemo/...` (also `-race`), `go vet ./proxy/dokodemo/`, `go run ./infra/vformat/main.go -mode check` pass with go1.27.0.

issues.title: FinalMask: Report TCP test write errors instead of hanging
issues.body:
### Problem

`mustSendRecvTcp` in `transport/internet/finalmask/tcp_test.go` calls `t.Fatal` from the writer goroutine, which `go vet` flags:

```
tcp_test.go:30: call to (*T).Fatal from a non-test goroutine
```

`t.Fatal` ends that goroutine via `runtime.Goexit`, so `close(waitCh)` never runs and the helper's final `<-waitCh` blocks until the package test timeout, losing the write error with it. The helper is also called with a zero-length message, where `io.ReadFull(to, buf[:0])` returns immediately, so nothing on the read side masks a failing write.

### Fix

Send the error over `waitCh`, which is already declared `chan error`, and check it on the test goroutine. The channel is buffered so the writer still cannot block, matching the previous `close`. This is the pattern already used by `TestTCPcustomClientRejectsMismatchedServerSequence` and `TestTCPWrapListenerRejectsImmediateWrapErrors` in this file.

`mustSendRecv` in `udp_test.go` and `mustSendRecvUDP` in `header/custom/state_test.go` use `t.Error`, which is safe from a goroutine, so they are unchanged.

### Verification

Forcing a write failure in the helper hangs the package for the full timeout before this change, and fails in 0.00s with the error after it. `go vet ./...` no longer reports the finding, and the package passes under `-race` and at `-count=30`.

issues.title: Fix noise after udphop
issues.body:
Fix noise emission when `noise` and `udphop` are used together.

Previously, noise state was keyed by the destination passed to `WriteTo`. udphop could replace that destination internally or switch the source socket without invalidating the noise state. Continuous outgoing traffic also refreshed the noise reset timeout, allowing repeated hops without another noise sequence.

**Implementation**

- Add shared `UDPPath` state through the existing finalmask dialer, containing the actual destination, a generation counter, and a mutex.
- Increment the generation after a successful hop changes the local endpoint, destination IP, or destination port.
- Have the noise wrapper clear its cached reset state when it observes a new generation. The next write emits noise before its payload, then resumes the existing reset behavior.
- Serialize the complete masked write against hopping, keeping all noise packets, configured delays, and the associated payload on the same socket and destination.

Generation tracking also handles returning to a previously used endpoint. Failed hops retain the active path and generation; attempts that leave the endpoints unchanged do not trigger additional noise.

Both configured noise items and Lua scripts use the existing emission code. Mask ordering, socket deadline propagation, receive handling, and connection cleanup remain unchanged. The existing connection stays in place, preserving Hysteria continuity. No configuration fields are added.

**Regression coverage**

- Source-port-only, destination-port-only, destination-IP-only, and combined changes.
- Continuous traffic, repeated writes on one path, and returning to a previous endpoint.
- Unchanged endpoints and failed hops.
- Concurrent hopping during delayed noise emission.
- Configured items and Lua scripts, mask ordering, reset behavior, deadline propagation, and socket cleanup.

**Verification**

- Focused noise/udphop tests and race detection passed.
- Finalmask and Hysteria package checks passed in short mode.
- GitHub’s formatting/protobuf check passed after applying the repository formatter.
- The full package run timed out in the separate Sudoku end-to-end harness; that run did not complete.

Keep the started gRPC server in the API goroutine
issues.body:
Stopping an API-enabled Xray instance immediately after `Start` can panic in `grpc.Server.Serve`. The serving goroutine reads `c.server` after `Close` has stopped the server and cleared the field. Both direct `api.listen` and tagged API listeners use this goroutine.

The regression uses real `core.New`, `Start`, and `Close` calls for both API configurations. It runs immediate start/stop cycles on one logical processor and yields to the API goroutine after shutdown. Each mode separately reproduces the nil receiver panic on the previous implementation.

Both regression cases pass on Windows and on Linux with `-race`. `go vet ./app/commander` passes on both platforms. The existing `TestCommanderListenConfigurationItem` and `TestCommanderRemoveHandler` integration tests also pass on Windows, exercising service registration and RPC calls for both listener modes.

issues.body:
Let's use #7355 to fix write interruption in both client and server Mux. #7359 solves the same problem with a different wrapper and removes the MutexWriter this proposal uses.

issues.title: Observatory: fix data race in observation results
issues.body:
## Summary

Fix a data race in ordinary Observatory's `GetObservation` by returning an independent snapshot of the observation results.

## Problem

`GetObservation` currently returns a new `ObservationResult` containing references to the observer's internal status slice and messages.

Background probes update these statuses under `statusLock`, while consumers may read or serialize them after `GetObservation` returns.

This can cause concurrent reads and writes in routing strategies, metrics, and gRPC protobuf serialization.

The issue was reproduced on the current upstream `main` with Go's race detector, including a protobuf serialization error:

```text
WARNING: DATA RACE
size mismatch: calculated=22, measured=31
```

## Solution

Deep-clone the observation result while holding the existing `statusLock`:

```go
o.statusLock.Lock()
defer o.statusLock.Unlock()

return proto.Clone(&ObservationResult{Status: o.status}), nil
```

This ensures that callers receive an independent snapshot, including nested protobuf messages and unknown fields.

The existing synchronization mechanism, protobuf API, health checks, and routing behavior remain unchanged.

## Testing

Added two regression tests:

- **Snapshot isolation:** verifies that returned results do not share mutable state with the observer or other snapshots, including nested messages and unknown fields.
- **Concurrent access:** exercises status updates, additions, removals, and concurrent reads with protobuf serialization.

Both tests reproduce the original issue. The snapshot test also fails when using a mutex without deep copying.

Validation completed successfully:

- `go test -race ./app/observatory/...`
- `go test ./app/observatory/... ./app/router/... ./app/metrics/...`
- Xray build
- Formatting and diff checks

## Performance

Deep cloning introduces O(n) copying under the existing mutex. Benchmarks covering 2, 20, and 200 outbound statuses confirm the expected linear cost.

The fix intentionally favors correctness and minimal changes over additional synchronization complexity.

issues.title: XHTTP: packet-down in stream-down with downlink keep-alive
issues.body:
# XHTTP: packet-down in stream-down with downlink keep-alive

Follows RPRX's packet-down design in https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/pull/6755#issuecomment-5720463978, which was written while closing the earlier downlink-resume attempt (#6755). That attempt was rejected because "restore connection" is too complex, with latency, ACK and so on. This one does not attempt connection restoration at all. No reconnection, no state machine, nothing to tune: each stream-down GET stays a single request; if the GET dies, the connection dies the ordinary way.

## Problem (from #4846)

CDNs kill a stream-down GET on body inactivity. This matters during uploads: with packet-up the uplink posts keep flowing, but the downlink proxy payload only arrives while the origin sends, so during a pure upload the GET idles and gets cut. Same story for any target that goes quiet for a while after responding.

## What this PR adds

When enabled on both ends, the stream-down response body is cut into packet-down frames with the five elements from the design comment:

- omittable session id excerpt: first 8 bytes of the session id, present on data and keep-alive frames (absent in stream-one where the session id is empty)
- omittable packet seq: uint64, counting data/keep-alive frames per stream-down GET
- mandatory type: data or padding
- mandatory length: uint16
- payload

Use today is the first one from the design comment: downlink keep-alive. While the downlink has been idle for a whole period, the server writes a padding frame (base62, in the spirit of tokenish x-padding) instead of staying silent. Everything the dispatcher sends rides in data frames, which is what lets the client tell padding apart from payload safely; the seq keeps the format ready for the future uses listed in the design comment (retransmission, multi-path-down) without another wire change.

h1, h2 and h3 are covered, since the framers sit on the body, not on a specific transport. stream-one gets the same treatment on its single response body. Browser dialer is out of scope for now: it has no place to read the response header that confirms the framing.

## Negotiation

Strictly opt-in and per request, so old servers are unaffected and nothing breaks behind middleboxes:

1. client config has packetDown: XHTTP stream requests not used as pure uplink (stream-down GET, stream-one request) carry X-Packet-Down: 1
2. server has packetDown configured and sees the marker: it answers with X-Packet-Down: 1 on the response, and frames; without the confirmed header the client never parses frames
3. any other combination: byte-identical wire format as today

## Config

```jsonc
"xhttpSettings": {
  "path": "/sh",
  "packetDown": {              // absent = disabled, as today
    "keepAlive": true,
    "keepAlivePeriod": "10-30",  // seconds; padded when inactive this long. defaults to 10-30
    "keepAliveLength": "24-64"   // padding size. defaults to 24-64
  }
}
```

Server side is the same block in the inbound; the server only honors the feature when the client asks.

## Not in this PR (deliberately)

- obfs of the frames (later, per the design comment)
- retransmission, multi-path-down, same-packet racing, ACK: the format carries seq and the session excerpt, but none of the machinery, exactly like packet-up carries seq today without using it
- nothing about #4846's larger downlink freeze problem (the 15-20 KB per TCP connection cut): this only discards the CDN idle timer, it does not split data across connections

## Tests

- packet_down_test.go: frame round trip (with/without excerpt, with/without seq), byte-stream shaped like a socket, splitting payloads larger than one frame, padding skipped, malformed frame rejected, keep-alive written when idle, keep-alive suppressed while active, config normalization
- splithttp_test.go: full listen/dial round trip with packet-down on both end (100 KiB), and the fallback case with the client setting present but the server without one
- infra/conf: JSON un

issues.title: Issue with terminating dead connections
XHTTP client: Add `scMaxPostRetries` to resend failed packet-up uploads
issues.body:
## Why

packet-up is there for CDNs and proxies that don't pass a streaming upload, so every packet goes through them as its own POST. Today the first POST that fails closes the whole connection, with everything that runs inside it. Behind a CDN a single 502 or 504 is not rare even when the server is fine, the CDN may time out waiting for the origin or lose its connection to it. An ordinary HTTP client would just send such a request again. Here it is safe to, since every packet carries its seq and with #7370 the server drops duplicates. It can't be done higher up, VLESS and mux don't see the packets.

One example we measured. With Yandex Cloud CDN about 2% of requests got a 504 after the CDN waited 5 seconds for the origin, and some got a 502. 3 of 10 uploads up to 3 MB broke with the current client and all 10 went through with resending. On a CDN emulator that checks integrity it was 12 of 12 against 4 of 12.

## What changed

- New client option `scMaxPostRetries`, 0 by default. Above 0, a packet that is not answered with 200 is sent again up to `scMaxPostRetries` times before the connection is closed as it is today.
- A 504 from a CDN comes only after several seconds. So one more copy is sent when the last copy was fully written but got no answer in 2 seconds. The first 200 wins and the other copies are cancelled. A packet with no 200 in 30 seconds fails the connection.
- The server gives up once it holds more than `scMaxBufferedPosts` packets after a missing seq. So with resending on, seq N is sent only after seq N minus `scMaxBufferedPosts`/2 is answered.
- `PostPacket` now uses the context it is given. The normal path detaches it from the connection as before, and the resend path uses it to cancel copies that are no longer needed. A cancelled copy no longer marks the HTTP/2 client as closed, otherwise each resend would open a new connection.
- With `scMaxPostRetries` at 0 the upload loop works as before.

## Why it is off by default

A resent packet may reach the server twice, for example when the CDN delivered it and then timed out waiting for the answer. A server without #7370 may read that copy again and corrupt the stream, and the client cannot tell which server it talks to. So resending stays off unless the server is known to drop duplicates. It could become the default some releases later.

## Testing and limits

- New `Test_PacketUpRetriesFailedPost` puts an HTTP/2 proxy in front of the server that answers 502 to the first upload of seq 1. The echo goes through with `scMaxPostRetries` 2 and times out with 0.
- `go test ./transport/internet/splithttp/... ./infra/conf/...` passes, also with `-race`.
- Together with #7370 I also ran a proxy that forwards every third upload to the server and still answers 504, so duplicates do reach the server. The stream stays intact.
- Only packet-up. A stream-up or stream-one upload is one long request, and the client cannot know how much of it the server got.
- It does not help when the CDN fails the download GET.
- HTTP/1.1 `PostPacket` does not read the answer status, so there only failed writes are resent. The browser dialer has no write callback, so it only resends on errors.
- The extra copy after 2 seconds assumes the server answers soon after the body is written. On a slow uplink with large `scMaxEachPostBytes` the body may still sit in the socket buffer, and a copy is sent for nothing. Behind a CDN small posts are the norm, so this should be rare. 2 and 30 seconds are constants.

issues.title: XHTTP server: Drop resent packet-up uploads instead of reading them again
issues.body:
## Why

A packet-up upload can reach the server twice. A CDN or a reverse proxy may send a POST to the origin again after a timeout, and a client may resend a packet that got a 502 or 504 although it went through. The server already drops a copy of a seq it has fully read. It does not handle a copy that is in the queue while the first one is only partly read. `uploadQueue` pushes the unread rest of a packet back into the heap with the same seq, so the next `Read` may pop the full second copy and return it from the start. The stream is then silently corrupted, and nothing in the logs says why.

With this change a duplicate of any seq is dropped, whatever sent it. It also makes it safe for a client to resend failed uploads, which is #7371.

## What changed

- The unread rest of a packet is kept in `uploadQueue.partial` instead of going back to the heap, and `nextSeq` moves on as soon as the packet starts being read.
- Any other copy of that seq is then below `nextSeq` and is dropped by the existing check.

## Testing and limits

- New `Test_UploadQueueDropsDuplicateSeq` pushes seq 1 twice before seq 0 and reads with an 8 KiB buffer. On main it fails with a corrupted stream, with this change it passes.
- `go test ./transport/internet/splithttp/... ./infra/conf/...` passes, also with `-race`.
- Nothing changes for clients that do not resend.
- A copy that arrives before its seq is read still takes a place in the reorder heap and counts towards `scMaxBufferedPosts`.

issues.title: DNS outbound: End UDP sessions once their queries are answered
issues.body:
A UDP session of the DNS outbound never reads EOF, so it lasts until the inbound drops it or its idle timer fires. The timer looks for activity once per connIdle, so a session answered right away ends after two periods, ten minutes by default. The dokodemo-door inbound drops idle UDP after two to three minutes; the TUN inbound never does. Stub resolvers and dnsmasq usually send each query from a new source port, so every query holds a session with three goroutines that long.

On my test bench (linux/arm64, FakeDNS, 5000 queries at 50 per second, a new port per query) RSS grew from 40 MB to 187 MB through dokodemo-door and to 180 MB through TUN, where the goroutines were gone only ten minutes after the last query.

I count the queries a UDP session still owes an answer, hijacked or sent upstream. While any is open the session keeps connIdle, so a slow lookup is not cut; one second after the last answer it ends, which still leaves room for AAAA sent after A from the same socket. TCP, the session of Xray's own DNS client and a connIdle below one second work as before.

With this change the same load ends at 62 MB through dokodemo-door and 64 MB through TUN. TestUDPDNSSessionsEnd sends 200 A and MX queries, MX forwarded upstream, each from its own socket: on main they leave 600 goroutines behind; with this change they are gone a second after the last answer.

### Description

> 简述：在 v26.10.17（与 main 相同）中，如果 XDRIVE 客户端在下载中途消失（进程被杀或断网），服务端无法察觉：它会继续从目标读取，并把剩余的整个响应写入存储（复现中 20 秒内写入约 235 MiB、607 个对象）。这些对象要等服务端的 mux 子连接自行结束后才会被清理（约 2.7–13 分钟），期间该会话仍被持续 LIST 轮询。原因是 XDRIVE 既没有对端存活检测，也没有背压。

Version: v26.10.17 (`92ccc93`, the newest release and the same commit as current `main`), `network: "xdrive"`, `service: "local"`. XDRIVE is only in the pre-releases since v26.9.30; it is not in v26.3.27. The session logic involved does not depend on the backend, so remote backends behave the same way.

When an XDRIVE client disappears in the middle of a download (process killed, network lost, which is common for mobile clients), the server does not notice:

1. It keeps reading from the target and writes the whole remaining response into the storage. In the repro the client had received 22 MiB of a 256 MiB body; within 20 s after the client was killed the server wrote 246,869,084 bytes in 607 objects.
2. These objects stay until the server-side mux sub-connection ends on its own: about 2.7 min when the target closes the connection after the body, about 13 min with a keep-alive target. Meanwhile the dead session is still polled (about 2 LIST per second).
3. The server logs nothing after the client is gone, even at `debug`.

With a remote backend every abandoned download can upload hundreds of MiB into the storage account, consume API quota and leave the objects there for minutes.

If only the application connection is closed while the client stays alive (curl killed), the server stops writing within about 5 s and the folder is cleaned up, so the problem is specific to the peer disappearing.

| 256 MiB body at 16 MiB/s, `sessionTtlSeconds: 30` | storage at +30 s | +90 s | +180 s | server kept writing |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| download completes (control) | 0 B | 0 B | 0 B | no |
| client `kill -9` after ~2 s | 246,869,084 B / 607 objects | same | same | yes, the whole remaining body |
| client `SIGTERM` after ~2 s | 246,394,446 B / 515 objects | same | same | yes |
| curl killed, client alive | 0 B (one `.end`) | 0 B | 0 B | no, stopped within ~5 s |
| client `kill -9`, keep-alive target, watched 900 s | 246,453,796 B | same | same | yes; empty only at ~750–780 s |
| client `kill -9`, target sends `Connection: close` | 246,485,923 B | same | 0 B | yes; empty at ~165 s |

- `Listener.claim` marks the session active (`transport/internet/xdrive/xdrive.go:225`); the mark is removed only in the connection's `onClose` (`xdrive.go:234`). `collect()` skips active sessions (`xdrive.go:267-269`), so the folder of a dead session is not collected while the server-side connection is open.
- That connection is closed only when the inbound handler returns (`app/proxyman/inbound/worker.go:123-127`), i.e. after the server-side mux session ends. XDRIVE has no peer liveness signal: no heartbeat, no idle timeout. `Conn.receive` blocks on the reader channel (`conn.go:53-61`), `walReader.poll` returns quietly on an empty listing (`wal.go:295-297`), `holeTimeout` fires only when later segments exist (`wal.go:312-321`), EOF comes only from a `.end` object (`wal.go:365`).

> 简述：v26.9.8 起使用 Go 1.27 构建，x/net http2.Transport 改为包装 net/http.Transport。当 TLS 握手被阻断而挂起时，每个会话都会新建一条 TCP 连接，XMUX 的 maxConnections 实际失效，连接数和内存随会话数线性增长。使用 `-tags http2legacy` 构建可恢复正常。与 #6644 不同，这里的额外连接与 MaxConcurrentStreams 无关。

Since v26.9.8 Xray is built with Go 1.27 (`fd2ca748`, "go.mod: Specify Go 1.27.x"); the v26.9.9 release binary reports `go1.27.1`, and the release workflow builds without extra tags. With Go 1.27, `golang.org/x/net` (v0.58.0 in v26.9.9, v0.59.0 on main) compiles `http2/transport_wrap.go`:

```go
//go:build go1.27 && !http2legacy
// Transport wrapping a net/http.Transport.
```

In this mode `http2.Transport.RoundTrip` is delegated to an internal `net/http.Transport` instead of x/net's own `clientConnPool`. The old pool deduplicated in-flight dials per address (`p.dialing[addr]`), so an XMUX client whose handshake hangs held exactly one socket and all further requests waited on it. The new path does not: while no HTTP/2 connection to the host is established yet, every waiting request dials its own TCP connection.

Normally this is invisible — the first handshake completes in one RTT and everything is multiplexed afterwards. But when handshakes hang (e.g. a middlebox blackholes the flow after the ClientHello — the TSPU scenario from #6376), **every proxied session gets its own TCP connection**. `xmux.maxConnections` still limits the number of XMUX clients (the debug log below shows two `XMUX: creating xmuxClient` lines and no removals), but not the dials underneath them.

- `maxConnections: 2`/`3`, introduced as the anti-TSPU default (`18e28390`, #6376), no longer keeps the client under the ~4-connection limit — it opens hundreds or thousands of connections and keeps re-triggering the ban;
- memory grows linearly with hung sessions; in a memory-limited container the process is OOM-killed, taking every other (healthy) outbound down with it.

issues.title: panic: slice bounds out of range [8192:8171] in XtlsPadding (VLESS outbound, Reality + Vision), recurring ~6x/hour on 25.6.8 / 25.9.5 / 25.12.8
issues.body:
## Summary

A relay node (Xray terminates several inbounds and forwards everything through ONE VLESS+Reality+`xtls-rprx-vision` outbound to another Xray) crashes the whole process several times per hour with a negative-length `Extend` in `proxy.XtlsPadding`. All inbounds are dropped on every crash (about 1 s with `RestartSec=1`).

No `testseed` anywhere in the config (so this is not #5961's "invalid testseed" case). No mux: 0 `v1.mux.cool` connections in the log over 24 h.

## Panic (identical every time, only goroutine ids differ)

```
panic: runtime error: slice bounds out of range [8192:8171]

goroutine 640 [running]:
github.com/xtls/xray-core/common/buf.(*Buffer).Extend(...)
        github.com/xtls/xray-core/common/buf/buffer.go:153
github.com/xtls/xray-core/proxy.XtlsPadding(0xc00021f740, 0x0, 0xc0002e1a28, 0x1?, {0x19a0058, 0xc000254730}, {0xc000269200?, 0xc000730000?, 0xc00033fb40?})
        github.com/xtls/xray-core/proxy/proxy.go:519 +0x79e
github.com/xtls/xray-core/proxy.(*VisionWriter).WriteMultiBuffer(0xc0002e19e0, {0xc00047ea98, 0x1, 0x1})
        github.com/xtls/xray-core/proxy/proxy.go:390 +0x5dd
github.com/xtls/xray-core/common/buf.copyInternal(...)
        github.com/xtls/xray-core/common/buf/copy.go:99 +0x15a
github.com/xtls/xray-core/common/buf.Copy(...)
        github.com/xtls/xray-core/common/buf/copy.go:116
github.com/xtls/xray-core/proxy/vless/outbound.(*Handler).Process.func4()
        github.com/xtls/xray-core/proxy/vless/outbound/outbound.go:360 +0xc79
```

(v25.12.8, go1.25.5, linux/amd64, kernel 6.8, 1 vCPU. `Process.func3` on 25.6.8 — same frames.)

## Analysis

The high bound `8171` is exactly `buf.Size - 21`. In `XtlsPadding`:

```go
if paddingLen > buf.Size-21-contentLen {
    paddingLen = buf.Size - 21 - contentLen
}
...
newbuffer.Extend(paddingLen)
```

`[8192:8171]` means `newbuffer.end == 8192` and `paddingLen == -21`, i.e. `contentLen == 8192`: a full 8192-byte block reached `XtlsPadding` unsplit. `Extend` has no check for negative `n`, so `b.v[b.end:end]` panics with low > high (the `end > len` check only guards the upper side).

`ReshapeMultiBuffer` is supposed to prevent this (it splits every block with `Len() >= buf.Size-21`), and `VisionWriter.WriteMultiBuffer` calls it right before the loop, so a full block should not get through. I could not find the path by reading the code (`XtlsPadding` and `ReshapeMultiBuffer` are byte-identical in v25.12.8 and v26.11.9). Possibilities I could not exclude: a buffer that is mutated/re-used between `ReshapeMultiBuffer` and `XtlsPadding` (pool double-release?), or a block larger than `buf.Size` entering through a non-standard reader.

Cheap hardening regardless of root cause: clamp `paddingLen` at 0 (`if paddingLen < 0 { paddingLen = 0 }`) and/or reject `n < 0` in `Buffer.Extend`. That would turn a process-wide crash into a (harmless) missing padding. Note that `newbuffer.Write(b.Bytes())` also silently truncates if `contentLen + 21 > 8192`, so the root cause is worth fixing too.

## Environment / what was tried

- Topology: several inbounds (Reality-TCP-Vision, Reality-TCP-Vision with self-steal dest, XHTTP+TLS, gRPC+TLS) → one VLESS+Reality+Vision outbound → Xray 25.6.8 server.
- Panics occur with users of ALL four inbounds (so not specific to one inbound transport).
- Versions tried as the relay: 25.6.8 (~1 panic / 5–10 min), 25.9.5 (2 in 1h20m), 25.12.8 (~6 / hour, 434 in 3 days, clustered: up to 5 within a minute). Not yet tried: 26.x on this node (26.10.31/26.11.9 server side breaks sing-box Reality clients in our tests, so we cannot deploy it for production users).
- Config has no `testseed`; `flow: xtls-rprx-vision` only.
- Related: #2651 (same signature, fixed in 2023), #5961 (same signature on 26.2.6/26.3.27, closed with "don't set testseed"), #6072.

## Expected

No process-wide panic on any input to the Vision writer.

Sockopt: Report the real ioctl error from OriginalDst on Darwin
issues.body:
### Problem

`OriginalDst` in `transport/internet/sockopt_darwin.go` reports success when the `DIOCNATLOOK` ioctl fails:

```go
if _, _, errno := syscall.Syscall(syscall.SYS_IOCTL, fd, DIOCNATLOOK, uintptr(unsafe.Pointer(&nl))); errno != 0 {
	return net.IP{}, -1, os.NewSyscallError("ioctl", err)
}
```

`err` is the `os.Open("/dev/pf")` result from the top of the function, which already returned early if it was non-nil, so `err` is always `nil` here — and `os.NewSyscallError` returns `nil` for a nil error. The `errno` the ioctl returned is dropped.

Both callers (`tcp.GetOriginalDestination`, `udp.RetrieveOriginalDest`) only test `err != nil`, so they build a destination from the zero IP and port `-1`: `net.IPAddress(net.IP{})` returns a nil `Address`, `net.Port(-1)` wraps to 65535, and `IsValid()` does not catch it since it only checks `Network != Network_Unknown`.

### Fix

Report `errno`. It is already the branch condition, so the error is always non-nil.

### Notes

Two further issues in this function, left alone because Darwin's `struct pfioc_natlook` cannot be verified (no `net/pfvar.h` in the SDK) and the path has no test coverage: `nl.proto` is always `IPPROTO_TCP` although `hub_darwin.go` reaches this function for UDP, and `nl.af` is never set to `AF_INET6` although the result is switched on `nl.af`. `sockopt_freebsd.go` sets both.

`go build ./...`, `go vet ./...`, `go run ./infra/vformat -mode check` and `go test ./...` are clean on this branch; the three geodata-dependent packages fail identically on unmodified `main` here because `geoip.dat` / `geosite.dat` are absent locally.

issues.title: XHTTP: Add configurable response headers
issues.body:
## What

Adds an optional `responseHeaders` map (`map<string, string>`) to the XHTTP inbound settings, giving the server control over the headers it writes on responses.

Currently the hub hardcodes a set of response headers: the CORS block for the browser dialer (`Access-Control-Allow-Origin`, `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials`, `Access-Control-Allow-Methods`, `Access-Control-Allow-Headers`), `X-Accel-Buffering`, `Cache-Control` and the SSE `Content-Type`. With `responseHeaders` an operator can add, override, or remove any of them, as well as set arbitrary extra response headers.

## Semantics

- A key that doesn't collide with a default header is added to every response.
- A key that matches a hardcoded header overrides it.
- An empty value removes that header from the response entirely (including the hardcoded ones).
- When `responseHeaders` is unset, the behavior is byte-identical to before.

Example:

```json
"xhttpSettings": {
  "path": "/api/v2/stream",
  "responseHeaders": {
    "Server": "nginx",
    "Cache-Control": "no-cache, no-transform",
    "Access-Control-Allow-Origin": "https://example.com",
    "X-Accel-Buffering": ""
  }
}
```

## Why

- The CORS headers only matter for the browser dialer; a plain server deployment currently emits `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` on every response, which is undesirable behind a specific origin and gets flagged by security reviews.
- Reverse-proxy and CDN setups sometimes require specific response headers (`Server`, `Via`, custom headers) or different cache semantics.
- Operators running behind intermediaries may want the response header set to stay consistent with the profile of the service they front, instead of carrying markers that no other service on that endpoint emits.

## Notes

- Server-side only; the client ignores it. It round-trips through `extra` like the other settings.
- `config.pb.go` regenerated with protoc v6.33.5 / protoc-gen-go v1.36.11 — the header matches all existing `.pb.go` files (`check-proto` passes; I verified the unmodified proto regenerates byte-identical with this toolchain first).

## Tests

- `Test_SetResponseHeader`: default / override / removal via empty value.
- `Test_WriteResponseHeader_ResponseHeaders`: CORS default, override, removal, custom header addition, origin echo.
- `go test ./...` passes locally across all packages, except the pre-existing network-dependent `TestQUICNameServer` in `app/dns`, which fails identically on pristine `main` in my environment (no QUIC egress).

issues.title: TUN inbound: Route each new UDP destination, keeping FullCone NAT within a route
issues.body:
The UDP FullCone table (#5509) is keyed by the source only, and only the first packet of a session is routed, so later destinations of that source reuse its outbound. As the TUN never sees a socket close, a port that the OS reuses before the session expires inherits the old route. For example, DNS on a port last used by a direct or blocked flow never reaches the DNS outbound, and a resolver that retries from the same port (mDNSResponder) keeps the stale session alive.

Now a new destination is routed once, with fake IPs judged by their domain and no DNS lookup made. It then joins its source's session for the same rule, or gets a session of its own. Destinations of one rule still share a session, so FullCone is kept within a rule, and a balancer picking another outbound doesn't split it. Routing runs off the goroutine that reads the tun. WireGuard and MASQUE servers are unchanged.

Checked on a real utun on macOS with the system resolver: DNS on a reused port is answered and destinations of one rule leave from one port, while on main the DNS goes nowhere and every destination leaves from the first one. A new destination costs about 2 µs more; established flows and throughput are unchanged.

AI disclosure: this PR was completed using Claude Opus 5.5.

issues.title: tun: end UDP flows and cancel dispatches when the inbound closes
issues.body:
## Problem

Closing a core instance that has a `tun` inbound leaves its UDP flows alive, and everything they hold with them.

- `Handler.Init` detaches the handler's context from the instance (`core.ToBackgroundDetachedContext`), and nothing cancels it on `Close`.
- `stack.Close` resets the TCP connections and closes the sockets opened by `DialUDP`, but never touches the UDP flow table (`udpConnectionHandler.udpConns`).

So each UDP flow's reader keeps waiting on its packet queue after `Close`, which pins its XUDP mux session, the mux `ClientWorker` and that worker's connection to the server.

Measured in a client that embeds the tun inbound and restarts the instance per session (goroutine origins from `runtime.Stack`): about 80 goroutines, 0.8 MB of live heap and stacks, and one established outbound connection leaked per instance, with no decay over 8+ minutes. After 25 instances: 1600 goroutines, all created by `tun.(*udpConnectionHandler).HandlePacket`, `mux.(*ClientWorker).Dispatch`, `mux.NewClientWorker` and `mux.(*DialingWorkerFactory).Create`, and 17 established connections to the server.

## Fix

- `Handler` owns a `cancel` for its detached context and calls it in `Close` before closing the stack, so in-flight dispatches unwind (also the ones not blocked on the reader).
- `stack.Close` ends every UDP flow (`udpConnectionHandler.closeAll`): their readers get EOF, the dispatches return and release their outbounds. The flow table also refuses new flows from then on, mirroring `handleTCP`'s `closed` check: a packet already in flight between the stack closing and the tun closing used to open a fresh flow (and, with a mux outbound, dial a worker) during shutdown.

The remaining XUDP mux workers then close on the mux client's idle check (two 16 s monitor ticks after their last session), after which goroutines and heap are back at the baseline and no server connections remain.

## Verification

- New tests: `TestUDPHandlerCloseAllEndsFlows` (flows end on close, a late packet opens none) and `TestHandlerCloseCancelsDispatches` (a dispatch that is not reading returns when the handler closes). `go test -race ./proxy/tun/` passes.
- With the patch, 20 instance start/stop cycles end with 0 established connections to the server and the baseline goroutine count; without it, 17 connections and 1600 goroutines that never go away.

issues.title: Metrics: Close HTTP connections when stopping Xray `Instance`
issues.body:
When an application embeds Xray and restarts an `Instance`, an HTTP collector can keep using its existing metrics keep-alive connection after `Instance.Close()`. The old handler remains available instead of the collector reconnecting to the new instance. This affects both direct `metrics.listen` and connections routed to `metrics.tag`.

`http.Serve` creates an HTTP server that the metrics handler does not retain. Closing its listeners stops new accepts, but leaves accepted connections open. Retain one `http.Server` for both listeners and close it with the metrics handler, while keeping the existing explicit listener cleanup. Capture the server before starting either serving goroutine so an immediate close is also handled.

The regression starts actual core instances, makes a successful HTTP/1.1 request, calls `Instance.Close`, then checks that the same connection can no longer receive any HTTP response. It covers `listen`, `tag`, and both together; all three fail against the original production code. Fixtures use only a loopback listener and in-memory connections.

issues.title: XDNS finalmask: `tcp://` resolvers send unframed queries; a domain like `t.example.com.` crashes the client
issues.body:
### Integrity requirements

- [x] I have read all the comments in the issue template and ensured that this issue meet the requirements.
- [x] I confirm that I have read the documentation, understand the meaning of all the configuration items I wrote, and did not pile up seemingly useful options or default values.
- [x] I provided the complete config and logs, rather than just providing the truncated parts based on my own judgment.
- [x] I searched issues and did not find any similar issues.
- [x] The problem can be successfully reproduced in the latest Release

### Description

Two bugs in the XDNS client, both from #6718. Reproduced with v26.10.31 built from the tag (a4a3dff, go1.27.3); the three files involved are unchanged on `main`.

**1. `tcp://` resolvers send DNS messages without the two-byte length prefix**

`transport/internet/finalmask/xdns/resolver_tcp.go:127`:

```go
_ = binary.Write(r.conn, binary.BigEndian, len(p))
_, _ = r.conn.Write(p)
```

`binary.Write` takes only fixed-size values. Given an `int`, it returns `binary.Write: some values are not fixed-sized in type int` and writes nothing, and the error is dropped. So each query goes out bare. A DNS server reads the random query ID as the length (RFC 1035 §4.2.2, RFC 7766 §8) and never answers. Against a `miekg/dns` TCP server, `TCPResolver` gets no reply within 5 s; a `dns.Client{Net: "tcp"}` asking the same question does get one. Reading answers (`recv`) handles the prefix correctly.

Possible fix, a single write as RFC 7766 §8 recommends:

```go
b := make([]byte, 2+len(p))
binary.BigEndian.PutUint16(b, uint16(len(p)))
copy(b[2:], p)
_, _ = r.conn.Write(b)
```

**2. A domain with an empty label, or a label over 63 bytes, passes the config check and then panics the process**

`NewDomain` (`domain.go:82`) rejects only `..` and builds the name with `dnsmessage.NewName(domain + ".")`, which checks only the total length. So `t.example.com.` (trailing dot), `a.`, `.a`, `.`, an empty name and a 64-byte label are all accepted, by `xray run -test` too. On the first packet, `client.go:152` calls `common.Must2(msg.AppendPack(buf[:0]))`. Packing fails with `zero length segment` or `segment length too long`. The panic, in mKCP's updater goroutine, makes the process exit with status 2. `Must2`'s own comment says that errors user input can cause must be handled.

`NewDomain` already computes `ascii, err := idna.ToASCII(domain)` and trims its dots, then never uses it. Building the name from `ascii` would make `t.example.com.` mean `t.example.com`. It would also fix IDN names, which now go on the wire as raw UTF-8: `тест.рф.` instead of `xn--e1aybc.xn--p1ai.`, the name the zone is delegated under. An empty result and labels over 63 bytes would still need rejecting, for example:

```go
ascii = strings.Trim(ascii, ".")
if ascii == "" {
	return nil, errors.New("empty domain")
}
for _, label := range strings.Split(ascii, ".") {
	if len(label) == 0 || len(label) > 63 {
		return nil, errors.New("invalid domain")
	}
}
name, err := dnsmessage.NewName(ascii + ".")
```

The server calls `NewDomain` too, so for IDN names both sides would change together. If `send` handled the `AppendPack` error instead of using `Must2`, a bad name would drop the packet and the process would keep running.

With both changes applied, `go test ./transport/internet/finalmask/xdns/` still passes. `TCPResolver` then gets the `miekg/dns` server's answer, and a client for `t.example.com.` sends its queries instead of panicking.

### Reproduction Method

issues.title: Wait for log writers to close on shutdown
issues.body:
On Windows, an application that shuts down Xray and immediately renames its log file can get a sharing violation. `Close` signals the log worker, which releases the file later when it exits.

Wait for the worker to release the writer before returning from `Close`. Ignore messages received after shutdown and check for shutdown again when acquiring the worker permit. In `app/log`, detach both handlers before waiting so a worker can finish formatting a message that itself records a log. Keep `Start` and `Close` serialized.

The regressions hold a real file writer open during message formatting, rename the file as soon as `Close` returns, and check that a late message cannot create another writer. Both regressions fail on the previous implementation. The Windows run reproduces the sharing violation.

`Close` can now wait for in-flight formatting and writes to finish. The message queue remains best effort.

Windows and Linux each passed all 14 tests in `./common/log`, `./app/log`, and `./app/log/command`. The Linux run used `-race`. `go vet` passed for all three packages on both platforms, and the Windows main build passed.

AI-assisted implementation and tests.

issues.title: Geodata: Retain successful asset updates when another asset fails
issues.body:
When a scheduled GeoIP/GeoSite update loses a configured category in one asset, keep successful updates to the other asset. For example, a bad GeoSite release should not prevent fresh GeoIP data from remaining installed on disk and in live matchers, including after the next restart.

Apply each already-downloaded asset independently. Commit it if the existing registries reload successfully. Otherwise restore only that asset, reload the restored files, retain the error, and continue to later assets. This preserves successful updates in either configured asset order. Stop if a swap, file rollback, or recovery reload fails; a backup-cleanup error does not roll back an already accepted update.

Eight synthetic HTTPS regression cases cover missing GeoSite/GeoIP/both categories and successful updates, in both asset orders. They independently check each file and each live matcher. The four partial-success cases fail on the previously submitted implementation.

Validation:
- Windows Go 1.27.3: all 66 tests in `./app/geodata ./common/geodata` pass, with no skips; scoped `go vet` and main build pass.
- Linux Go 1.27.1 / CGO: the same 66 tests pass with `-race`, with no skips; scoped `go vet` and main build pass.
- Repository format check passes on the exact Git source archive.
- Existing tests use checksum-verified public CI GeoIP-lite/GeoSite assets from release 20261110012153; new update fixtures are synthetic and use a trusted local HTTPS test server.
- The full repository suite and macOS runtime were not run locally.

Downloads are still staged before any asset is changed. Recovery is per asset, including when a file is used by multiple registries; this does not promise per-registry partial acceptance of one shared file or global atomicity. The tradeoff is one full registry reload per accepted asset instead of one per bundle, plus recovery reloads for rejected updates.

Implemented and tested with Codex assistance.

issues.title: Hysteria inbound: Close a removed user's connections
Hysteria inbound: Fix `RemoveUser` not taking effect on authenticated connections
issues.body:
A Hysteria client authenticates once per QUIC connection. After `RemoveUser` the user is gone from the validator, but a connection that is already authenticated keeps opening new TCP streams and UDP sessions, so the removal does nothing until the client reconnects. With keepalive that can be hours.

The official server can drop such a client through `TrafficLogger` (`LogTraffic` returning false, which is what `/kick` uses). There is no counterpart for it here, while the WireGuard and MASQUE inbounds already end the session in `RemoveUser`.

This checks the user again when a stream or a UDP session is opened and closes the connection if the user has been removed. The client reconnects and fails auth. Connections authenticated by the transport `auth` (no `clients`) are not affected.

Tested on v26.11.9 with two users and `xray api rmu` / `adu`: before, the removed user keeps working over TCP and UDP; with this, its connection is closed on the next request, the other user is not affected, and it works again after being re-added.

issues.title: [Feature Request / Proposal] Preventing IP leaks during core restarts / profile switching with autoSystemWfpBlockLeak
issues.body:
Hello Xray-core maintainers and contributors!

First of all, thank you for the recent work on native Windows TUN. Moving leak protection directly into Xray via WFP is a huge step forward and allows GUI clients (like v2rayN) to rely entirely on native Xray TUN rather than legacy multi-core workarounds.

I would like to ask for your thoughts on an architectural edge case related to how GUI clients manage the `xray.exe` lifecycle, and whether addressing it within Xray-core aligns with your vision.

### The Scenario
When a user switches servers, updates routing/DNS profiles, or clicks "Restart Service" in a GUI client like v2rayN, the client terminates the current `xray.exe` process and spawns a new one.

Because the current WFP rules created by `autoSystemWfpBlockLeak` are tied to the dynamic WFP session (`FWPM_SESSION_FLAG_DYNAMIC`) of the running `xray.exe` process, the moment the old process exits, Windows immediately tears down the `xray_tun` adapter and removes the WFP filters. For the ~1–2 seconds it takes for the new `xray.exe` instance to initialize Wintun and re-apply `autoSystemRoutingTable` / `autoSystemWfpBlockLeak`, the OS falls back to the physical interface (direct), causing a brief IP/traffic leak.

### Possible Approaches
I am wondering what the maintainers think about bridging this restart gap natively in Xray. A couple of concepts come to mind:

1. **CLI-Managed / Companion WFP Lock:**
   Adding an optional flag or lightweight CLI subcommand (e.g., `xray tun-wfp lock` / `unlock`, or a helper mode bound to the parent GUI PID so it still utilizes `FWPM_SESSION_FLAG_DYNAMIC` for crash safety) that holds the baseline `"all"` / `"allexceptlan"` WFP block rules across worker restarts. This way, a GUI client could arm the WFP filter once when starting its session, restart `xray.exe` processes freely without dropping the WFP wall during the 1–2s gap, and disarm it on deliberate exit.

2. **Graceful Config Reloading for TUN:**
   While Xray already has gRPC APIs for dynamic outbound/routing updates, full profile switches in GUI clients often rewrite the entire config. Allowing `xray.exe` to reload its configuration on the fly (via API or signal) without destroying the active `wintun` adapter and its dynamic WFP session would eliminate both the Wintun recreation delay and the leak window.

### Question to Maintainers
How do you view this problem from Xray's design perspective?
1. Do you think bridging this restart gap belongs with in Xray-core, or do you consider it strictly the responsibility of external GUI clients?
2. If addressing it in Xray-core makes sense to you, what architectural direction would you prefer (one of the concepts above, or a completely different approach)?

If this aligns with the project's goals, I might be open to exploring the codebase further and perhaps drafting a PR for your review.

Thank you for your time!

comments.issue_title: DNS outbound: End UDP sessions once their queries are answered
comments.body:
Ran this branch against a hand-rolled upstream on Windows to check the counter. The teardown itself checks out: copying the PR's `TestUDPDNSSessionsEnd` onto `main` reproduces the leak exactly (`sessions are still open: 604 goroutines above the baseline`), and it passes on the branch in 2.03s. A 2.5s lookup is also not cut (answered in 2.501s), so the linger doesn't trade away slow answers.

One finding though: the pending count isn't correlated with query identity, and that costs an answer when the upstream emits a second datagram for a single query. One client socket, A answered immediately, AAAA answered after 3s:

| upstream behaviour | main | this branch |
|---|---|---|
| one datagram per query | AAAA at 3.001s | AAAA at 3.002s |
| A answer repeated 300ms later | AAAA at 3.002s | AAAA never arrives (8s timeout) |

Mechanism: `add()` runs once per parsed query, `done()` once per message read from `connReader`. The duplicate takes the count 2 -> 1 -> 0 while the AAAA query is still outstanding, the session drops to the 1s linger, and the answer that lands at 3s has nowhere to go. On main there is no count, so the 300s idle window absorbed the extra datagram.

Triggers are anything that emits a second datagram for one query — a forwarder racing two upstreams and relaying both, a server resending on its own timeout, a reflected copy — and the exposure is exactly the A+AAAA pair from one stub socket, which is the case the linger exists to allow.

Keying pending queries by ID (a `map[uint16]` or a set, ignoring an `add()` for an ID already pending) and decrementing on the response's parsed ID would remove the class rather than this instance; it costs a header parse in `response()`. If it helps, the probe is a self-contained `proxy/dns` test that fails on the branch and passes on main — I can send it as a patch for the regression case.

comments.issue_title: XHTTP: packet-down in stream-down with downlink keep-alive
comments.body:
Packet-down rides on the requests XHTTP already makes, so the path layout does not change:

- stream-down: `GET /yourpath/sameUUID` carries `X-Packet-Down: 1`; stream-one: `POST /yourpath/` carries it as well. The response headers it already sets (`X-Accel-Buffering`, `Cache-Control`, `Content-Type`) stay untouched.
- a server with `packetDown` configured answers with the same `X-Packet-Down: 1` and from there the body is frames: `flags:u8 type:u8 length:u16be [session id:8] [seq:u64be] payload`. Bit 0 of flags marks the 8-byte session id excerpt, bit 1 marks the 8-byte seq, type is 0x01 data or 0x02 padding, length counts payload bytes only, so the header is 4 bytes when neither optional field is there. stream-one has no session id, so it gets neither field.
- the only thing it does today is the downlink keep-alive: once the downlink has been idle for a whole `keepAlivePeriod` (10-30s default) the server writes one padding frame of `keepAliveLength` base62 bytes (24-64 default), and the client drops padding frames and ignores seq, which only counts data and padding frames inside this GET and is kept for retransmission and multi-path-down later.
- every other combination sends exactly the bytes it sends today.

comments.issue_title: VLESS: Run client Mux directly on its transport
comments.body:
@RPRX

This is the first working version for review, updated in `39bafa6`. All comparisons below are against upstream `f082058`.

Mux now lives in `proxy/vless/multiplex`, and Reverse in `proxy/vless/reverse`. VLESS inbound, outbound and Reverse call them directly. The old folders and the separate `outbound/mux.go` are removed. Configuration is now under VLESS `settings.multiplex`, and the main implementation names also use `multiplex`.

Client and server share frame parsing and connection lifecycle code. The old generic Mux connection machinery and duplicate shutdown paths are removed.

Ordinary child responses go through `DispatchLink` directly into the Mux encoder. Their individual response pipes and copy loops are removed. One sender per carrier serializes encoded frames through a bounded queue. When that queue is full, subsequent writes wait for space. END waits for the underlying write to complete before retiring the old session identity, preserving DATA/END order and valid ID reuse.

One receive pipe remains on each outgoing carrier so transport reads can proceed independently of frame parsing and delivery. The original thresholds remain: 64 KiB for ordinary connections and 16 KiB for Reverse. XUDP retains its own association queues for reconnection; the old binding stops reading before the new binding takes over. No new server session-count or rate limit is introduced.

Reverse no longer has duplicate initialization, the unused control-response buffer or a periodic collector for completed Portal handlers. Closing a handler removes that exact handler. Heartbeats and reconnection are retained.

Close and interruption now pass through the reader and UDP destination-override wrappers. Native timeout-capable readers use their existing timeout mechanism without an extra reader goroutine. Canceling a blocked XDrive write unblocks it; normal shutdown of an idle connection retains EOF.

Incoming VMess Mux compatibility is retained. The existing VMess UDP-cone path through `common/xudp` remains for now; its removal is deferred until the new implementation stabilizes. Legacy `mux` configuration must be replaced with `settings.multiplex`; the old SenderConfig Mux format is rejected with a migration message. The remaining classic Reverse binary-configuration path is removed, while native VLESS Reverse is retained.

Local Windows loopback measurements used both matching endpoints, six paired runs per workload, and byte-verified echo traffic. The single-stream workload transferred 512 MiB; the mixed workload transferred 1 GiB across eight bulk streams, with a small request/response stream sharing the carrier. Medians were:

- Single-stream throughput: **185 → 196 MiB/s**.
- Mixed-load throughput in the repeat series: **253 → 305 MiB/s**.
- Small-request p95 under mixed load: **28.1 → 19.9 ms**.
- Combined client/server CPU under mixed load: **9.97 → 9.38 CPU-seconds per GiB** of verified echo payload.
- Server Private Bytes under mixed load: **76.1 → 64.8 MiB**.

Non-generated production Go code against upstream `f082058`: **35 files, +1600/−1836 lines, net −236**. The complete PR diff shown by GitHub is **60 files, +2122/−2818 lines, net −696**.

comments.issue_title: DNS outbound: End UDP sessions once their queries are answered
comments.body:
Measurements from a long-lived Windows TUN session that match this PR's description. Posting them because the cost per
unit is measurable on a real box, in case it helps with review.

**Environment:** Windows 11, v2rayN 7.25.6, Xray 26.11.9 (`676eaf6`, go1.27.3 windows/amd64), TUN inbound
(`xray_tun`, MTU 1500, `autoSystemRoutingTable: ["0.0.0.0/0"]`), outbound VLESS + WS + TLS, `mux.enabled: false`
(so no XUDP). DNS config: two domain-scoped `119.29.29.29` servers plus the default `1.1.1.1`; routing had
`port 53, inboundTag tun -> dns` and `inboundTag dns-module -> proxy`. Session age at measurement: ~1 h 50 m.

**1. Fresh DNS lookups through the tun cost 11.2 s each, consistently**

```
20/20 fresh random-label A queries   11,167 - 11,511 ms
same name already cached                    275 ms
same query to the LAN gateway (no tun)      131 ms
nslookup (2 s timeouts)              fails outright, no answer
```

**2. The delay is UDP-specific, not the IP/neighbour/PMTU layer**

```
TCP connect to 1.1.1.1:53 through the tun      26 ms   (the stack answers the SYN itself)
UDP DNS query to the same address        11,200 ms   (same moment, same destination)
```

An explicit `-Server 1.1.1.1` query is slow too, which rules out Windows' smart multi-homed resolution as the cause.

**3. Sessions do not end**

```
after 20 fresh lookups:  xray sockets 15 -> 31, handles 335 -> 352, still 31 sockets 60 s later
```

That is ~1 socket held per lookup, matching "a UDP session of the DNS outbound never reads EOF … the TUN inbound
never does [drop idle UDP]".

**4. Tun flow/neighbour state accumulates for the session's life**

```
xray_tun IPv4 neighbours: 493 entries  (464 Stale, 19 Unreachable, empty link-layer address)
                          vs Windows' Neighbor Cache Limit of 256 per interface
destination cache:        486 entries
```

**5. For completeness: UDP through this same profile is unusable outside the tun as well**

SOCKS5 UDP-ASSOCIATE against the client's own mixed port, DNS query to 1.1.1.1:53 and 8.8.8.8:53: no answer within
60 s, twice each. That part may well be the server's UDP relay rather than the tun, but it means every DNS lookup had
to be rescued by retries.

**6. Effect of taking DNS off the UDP path (control, not a fix)**

Switching the default server to IP-literal DoH (`https://1.1.1.1/dns-query`) and letting that connection go out
outside the tunnel:

```
50 fresh lookups:  min 445 / median 485 / max 896 ms, zero outliers over 2 s
socket count afterwards: 42 -> 14 -> 8 within 80 s of idle (before, sockets stayed pinned)
tun neighbours after core restart: 61 (vs 493 on the 2 h session)
```

One cold lookup immediately after the core restart still cost 12.5 s while a fresh upstream TLS connection was
dialled; it did not recur over the following 65 queries.

If the 11 s is a distinct problem from the teardown issue this PR fixes (the shape matches 2dust/v2rayN#10439, A/AAAA
resolution ~10-11 s under TUN), say so and I will file it separately with a repro harness rather than pollute this
thread.

comments.body:
@RPRX

I am continuing to simplify the draft. In commit [2abab46](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/commit/2abab4674eae6625a6cb4c0b06b269705bad73f2), I included a small reduction that preserves the existing functionality, after comparing several ways to remove pipes and change how Link is used.

I removed the unused response buffer from the Reverse control session. It was created for replies, but nobody read from it. Incoming data on that side is now released through `buf.Discard`. Control-message transmission, session completion and reconnection are retained.

I also removed duplicate Bridge and Portal initialization. The shared constructors are now `NewBridge` and `NewPortal`. Legacy protobuf configuration is handled by `newLegacyBridge` and `newLegacyPortal`, using the same initialization.

Five unreachable lines following the error for the removed `legacy reverse` setting were deleted.

This commit touches **10 functions and one struct field**:

- `infra/conf/xray.go`: **+0/-5**, file length **758 → 753 lines**. Removed unreachable code after the unconditional return in `Config.Build()`.
- `proxy/vless/inbound/inbound.go`: **+1/-1**, **648 → 648 lines**. `Handler.GetReverse()` calls the shared `NewPortal`.
- `proxy/vless/outbound/outbound.go`: **+1/-1**, **491 → 491 lines**. `New()` calls the shared `NewBridge`.
- `proxy/vless/reverse/bridge.go`: **+5/-13**, **297 → 289 lines**. The constructors share initialization; legacy settings go through `newLegacyBridge`.
- `proxy/vless/reverse/portal.go`: **+7/-18**, **338 → 327 lines**. Simplified the constructors, removed the unused pipe from `NewPortalWorker()`, and removed the `reader` field and its interruption in `heartbeat()`.
- `proxy/vless/reverse/reverse.go`: **+2/-2**, **94 → 94 lines**. `Reverse.Init()` calls the legacy-configuration constructors.

In a separate construction/close measurement, the Reverse control worker went from **89 to 78 allocations**, with allocated bytes falling from approximately **13,647 to 13,032 bytes per operation**. This measures control-worker construction and cleanup.

Alternatives compared:

- **Direct receiving with no receive pipe.** In the local eight-stream comparison, median throughput fell from approximately **267 to 220 MiB/s**, and latency increased. Not included.
- **Explicit TCP receive-buffer sizes of 64/128/256 KiB.** Throughput was approximately **125/191/227 MiB/s**. They did not recover the loss.
- **Collecting an entire frame before delivering it.** Throughput rose to approximately **293 MiB/s**, but available data was held until the frame completed. The first version also retained excessive memory with small fragments. Compacting the buffers addressed memory usage, but the partial-frame delivery delay remained.
- **A simpler incremental stream-frame reader.** It did not recover throughput without the pipe. With the existing pipe, some runs showed a CPU improvement, but a consistent overall throughput/latency advantage was not established.
- **DispatchLink with direct child-response writes.** The first version stalled on a failed route when a physical write was blocked. The corrected version added **80 net lines** and changed traffic accounting on failed routes. I did not include that broader change in this cleanup.
- **Returning a prepared Link instead of waiting for readiness.** It added **31 net lines** and failed the shutdown case: a blocked child close could leave the physical connection open.

For now, direct transmission and one receive pipe remain. The other buffers have separate responsibilities, including backpressure, session termination and XUDP reassociation.

**This commit: 6 files, +16/-40, net -24 lines. The full PR against main `f082058`: 47 files, +1066/-845, net +221 lines.** The PR as a whole still does not reduce source size.

This remains a draft, and I am continuing to work on it. Comments, suggestions, ~~criticism~~.

comments.issue_title: VLESS: Run client Mux directly on its transport
comments.body:
@RPRX

This is a draft, still under development. I reworked it around your clarification: move Mux into VLESS and remove the old generic connection path.

Mux now lives in `proxy/vless/multiplex`. VLESS inbound, outbound and Reverse call it directly. VLESS owns its Mux/XUDP pools. Enabling `mux.cool` on other outbounds is rejected at startup. Compatibility with existing VMess Mux clients is retained.

On the transmit side, frames go directly through the VLESS codec. The receive side retains one existing `pipe`, allowing transport reads to run independently of frame parsing and delivery to child connections. This part of the existing buffering mechanism remains.

I compared several alternatives:

- Fully direct receiving lost about 15% of throughput and increased latency under load.
- Channel-based read-ahead and a wider ReadV vector recovered only part of that loss. Rebuilding the existing pipe's accumulation, backpressure and shutdown logic under a different name would add more code.
- Writing a whole input batch under one lock could let a large response occupy the shared writer for too long. The current implementation submits at most two existing 8 KiB frames per write, then releases the lock. It does not wait for another input batch.
- Increasing stream frames to 32 KiB did not provide enough benefit to justify changing the existing framing and increasing head-of-line blocking.
- I did not include the full VMess rewrite from #5143. It changes termination signalling and authenticated inbound-user timeout handling. Their existing behavior is retained here.

The bounded writes follow your concern in [#7345](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/pull/7345#issuecomment-6714114884). The receive buffer addresses the separate read/parse overlap measured above.

Direct writes also require an interruptible XDrive connection, so stopping Mux can unblock a write waiting on a full ring. A quiescent connection still closes with EOF. VLESS now closes its owned Mux pools and cancels unfinished connection creation during shutdown. The original receive-buffer thresholds are retained: 64 KiB for ordinary Mux and 16 KiB for Reverse.

I compared both updated endpoints with main `14df073` on Windows loopback. Six paired runs used eight bulk streams plus a small request/response stream sharing one carrier. Medians were:

- Throughput: approximately **264 → 276 MiB/s**.
- Small-request p95 under load: **27.6 → 23.5 ms**.
- Combined client/server CPU: approximately **9.96 → 9.73 CPU-seconds per GiB** of verified echo payload, roughly unchanged.
- Client Private Bytes in separate memory runs: **57.0 → 56.5 MiB**, a small difference.

Single-stream results varied substantially. These local measurements do not establish a speedup for every workload or transport.

The fixes from #7359 and #7375 are preserved. Ordinary transports default to concurrency 8 and keep explicit positive values. XDrive retains the minimum of 128. XUDP settings are unchanged. Retirement of `common/xudp` remains a later step after the new Mux stabilizes.

The full PR diff against main `14df073` is **32 files, +588/-502 lines, net +86**, including **11 file moves**.

This is the first working version. I am still working on it. Comments, suggestions, ~~criticism~~.

comments.issue_title: [Feature Request / Proposal] Preventing IP leaks during core restarts / profile switching with autoSystemWfpBlockLeak
comments.body:
Thank you for your reply, @RPRX!

Following your suggestion, I opened a feature request in v2rayN (2dust/v2rayN#10538) sharing your quote and proposing that they keep `xray.exe` running and switch nodes via Xray's API.

However, 2dust closed it as `not planned` with the following reply:
> 抱歉，没有此计划。
> xray core api 比较难用，我们不准备这么做

**Why existing GUI clients struggle with the current API:**
GUI clients like v2rayN are built around generating a complete `config.json` from scratch whenever a user switches a node (since switching a node often changes not only the proxy outbound, but also routing rules, `dns` servers/rules, `observatory`, etc.). Using the current granular gRPC commands (`ado`/`rmo`/`adr`/`rmr`) requires clients to manually diff configs across multiple services, and top-level modules like `dns` or `observatory` cannot currently be reloaded via gRPC at all.

**Idea / Question:**
To make it easy for GUI clients (and users) to keep the `xray` process resident, what do you think about supporting a high-level full-config reload (e.g., an API command like `xray api reload -c config.json` or similar)?

When called on a resident `xray` process, Xray could apply the new `config.json` in-place (or re-initialize the internal core instance from the new config) while preserving the existing `tun` adapter (`wintun` handle, routing table, and active dynamic WFP session) if the `tun` inbound settings haven't changed.

This way, GUI clients wouldn't need to deal with granular gRPC calls or rewrite their config generators — they could simply pass the newly generated `config.json` to the running `xray.exe` process without ever dropping the TUN interface or WFP protection. What are your thoughts on this?

issues.title: Stuck in infinite "Reconnecting..." loop when disconnecting OpenVPN over Cloak on Windows 11
issues.body:
Describe the bug
When using AmneziaVPN (version 4.8.19.0) on Windows 11 with the OpenVPN over Cloak protocol, the application fails to terminate the connection properly. Clicking the "Disconnect" button triggers an infinite "Reconnecting..." state in the UI. The only way to stop it is to kill the process via Task Manager.

To Reproduce

Select a server with OpenVPN over Cloak protocol.
Click Connect and wait for a successful connection.
Click Disconnect.
The status changes to "Reconnecting..." and stays in this state indefinitely.
Expected behavior
The connection should terminate immediately, and the UI should return to the "Disconnected" state.

Logs & Technical Details
Based on preliminary observation, the issue seems to be a race condition/state conflict between the Cloak transport and the OpenVPN client:

Upon manual disconnection, the OpenVPN instance appears to receive a connection-reset or similar signal from the Cloak layer.
Instead of interpreting the disconnect as a "Stop" command, the OpenVPN client treats it as an accidental drop and triggers a SIGUSR1 (soft restart).
The Amnezia GUI becomes stuck waiting for the process to exit, while the process is trying to re-establish the tunnel.
Environment:

AmneziaVPN Version: 4.8.19.0
OS: Windows 11
Protocol: OpenVPN over Cloak
Installation method: Standard Windows Installer (installed via Amnezia client).
Possible Workarounds/Fixes suggested:

Adding remap-usr1 SIGTERM to the OpenVPN client configuration to force exit on resets.
Implementing explicit-exit-notify 1 (for UDP) or adjusting keepalive / ping-restart timers to be less aggressive during the shutdown phase.
Ensuring the GUI sends a hard SIGTERM or taskkill equivalent to the OpenVPN process when the user clicks "Disconnect".

per session, and Go's HTTP/2 client holds a 512 KiB scratch buffer per such
stream for its whole lifetime. A heap profile from the extension showed
`http2.(*clientStream).writeRequestBody` at 34.5 MB (74 % of the Go heap) with
~70 sessions, which Instagram/Facebook open within a minute.

The extension now sets `xhttpSettings.mode = "packet-up"` when the mode is empty
or `auto`: each POST has a `Content-Length`, so the buffer is payload-sized and
transient. An explicit mode is left as is; the server accepts both modes.
iOS extension only.
